items.summary: Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq as ANT on 19 November, opening at $111.50 — 34% above its $83 IPO price — and briefly reaching a market valuation of around $2 trillion, the largest US IPO on record at $81.3B raised. The shares eased to near $96–100 by midday, but the debut makes Anthropic the first publicly traded company focused on frontier AI. The offering is expected to close on 20 November.
items.title: Anthropic debuts on Nasdaq as ANT, opening 34% above its $83 IPO price

related.label: US Commerce rule targets remote access to advanced chips via third-country data centres

items.summary: The US Bureau of Industry and Security's interim final rule 'Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors' took effect on 19 November on its Federal Register publication. It requires a licence when advanced chips serve a data centre giving China-, Macau- or other D:5-linked firms remote access to more than 12 million TPP of compute, adds destination licences for advanced-chip shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, and formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. Data centres already serving covered customers have 90 days to obtain a licence, and Nvidia's interim chief said the company is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data-centre products to China.
items.title: US remote-access chip rule takes effect, closing the rent-not-buy workaround

items.summary: Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic have backed work toward a single shared, machine-readable AI training opt-out signal in robots.txt, tied to the IETF's AI Preferences initiative and its draft token `__usage_ai-training`. The aim is one interoperable preference for publishers instead of separate crawler directives per provider, covering training use rather than use as a source for AI-generated answers. Microsoft says it will begin honouring the signal on 1 February 2027, and Google plans to roll out support in 2027 as the standard develops.
items.title: Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic back a shared AI training opt-out signal

related.label: Tencent launches Hy4 flash at $0.07 per 1M input tokens

items.summary: Tencent has published the open weights for Hy4 Flash — the standard build, an FP8-quantised build and a pre-trained base model — on Hugging Face, ModelScope and GitCode, a day after the model launched as API-only. The multimodal mixture-of-experts model has about 220B total parameters with roughly 12B active per token and a 1M-token context, and Tencent reports it runs office tasks at about one-twentieth the cost of the flagship Hy4. The weights use the custom Tencent Hy License 1.0 rather than a standard open-source licence, with a separate written licence required for large model-as-a-service operators.
items.title: Tencent open-sources Hy4 flash weights: 220B parameters, 12B active, 1M context

items.summary: RSIBench-Infra (arXiv:2611.24395) asks whether LLM agents can optimise their own training and inference infrastructure at production scale, moving beyond benchmarks that target single software layers such as kernels. A preview gives agents a fixed 10-hour wall-clock budget to deliver end-to-end performance gains across real training workloads. It is the most direct benchmark yet of recursive self-improvement at the infrastructure layer, though only a preview with no full results has surfaced so far.
items.title: RSIBench-Infra: can agents optimise their own training infrastructure at production scale?

items.summary: Toaster (arXiv:2611.23648) builds a nonlinear recurrent memory by cascading two linear memory layers with target propagation, letting language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. The authors report it can match attention's prediction quality and represent associations that a single matrix memory cannot. If the claim holds up, it is a step toward attention-free long-context models with constant memory.
items.title: Toaster: nonlinear memory from cascaded linear memories and target propagation

items.summary: Weight Space Programming for Vision Language Model Repair (arXiv:2611.23615) extends weight-space programming — a language model editing another network's weights directly, without gradients — from language models to vision-language models. The work follows MIT CSAIL's November demonstrations in which a frontier model repaired a looping small language model with a tiny targeted weight edit. Applying the same idea to multimodal models would make direct weight-level repair a general model-maintenance tool rather than a language-only curiosity.
items.title: Weight Space Programming for Vision Language Model Repair
